section.p: This guide covers runtime reconfiguration of the nginx.http object — the top-level HTTP subsystem accessible from JavaScript. It covers:
Reading HTTP subsystem state (servers[], sockets[], variables{}, hash-size parameters)
Provisioning new listening sockets (nginx.createSocket())
Wiring sockets into the HTTP pipeline (nginx.http.attach())
Managing server-name dispatch (addServer, removeServer, rebuildVhostDispatch, match)
Safe patterns for cross-worker propagation

For location-level operations see Guide 4 (Locations) [js-reconfig-guide-locations.adoc]. For server-level operations see Guide 5 (Servers) [js-reconfig-guide-servers.adoc]. For cross-worker coordination see Guide 2 (All Workers) [js-reconfig-guide-all-workers.adoc]. For snapshot/restore see Guide 3 (Checkpoint/Restore) [js-reconfig-guide-checkpoint.adoc].
Socket provisioning spans four phases. Phases A-D are all pre-fork (config phase / init_conf). Post-fork socket creation uses Phase F.

stanza.v: Phase C listener.addServer(srv) activates the listener
Phase D listener.addVirtualServer(srv) adds a virtual-host entry

section.p: The four-phase model exists because nginx’s listening-socket infrastructure, HTTP connection pipeline, and virtual-host hash are built up incrementally. Each addServer / addVirtualServer call triggers an inline hash rebuild so the new names are reachable immediately.
Creates a new TCP listening socket.
address — "host:port" string, e.g. "0.0.0.0:9000" or "[::]:443".
Phase A (pre-fork / init_conf) — calls socket(), bind(), and listen() directly in the master process. The socket is ready before any worker forks.

Phase F (post-fork, from a request handler) — sends the bind address to the manager thread via AF_UNIX + SCM_RIGHTS. The manager creates the socket in the master’s network namespace and delivers the file descriptor back to the requesting worker. Other workers obtain the same fd via sock.broadcast().
Member │ R/W │ Description
address │ R │ Bind address string, e.g. "0.0.0.0".
port │ R │ Bind port number.
fd │ R │ Raw file descriptor number.
listener │ R │ Associated NginxHttpListener, or null if attach() has not been called.
close() │ — │ Closes the socket file descriptor.
broadcast() │ — │ (Phase F) Delivers the socket fd to all other workers via the manager thread. Returns Promise<undefined>.

section.p: Distributes a post-fork socket file descriptor to every other worker in the nginx pool so that all workers can accept connections on the new port.
Worker-only. Throws InternalError if called from config phase.
Synchronous from the sender’s perspective — blocks until the manager has delivered the fd and acked.
Returns undefined (not a Promise).
In Phase A (pre-fork), nginx.createSocket() runs in the master process. The OS socket is created before fork(), so every worker inherits the same fd automatically.

In Phase F (post-fork), a worker asks the manager thread to create the socket. The manager creates it in the master’s network namespace and returns the fd via SCM_RIGHTS to the requesting worker only. Every other worker has its own separate fd table and knows nothing about the new socket until sock.broadcast() is called.
sock.broadcast() goes through four sub-phases:

stanza.v: ngx_js_sw_manager_start() creates one socketpair per worker:
Workers inherit [1] on fork; master keeps [0].
Manager: bind+listen → sends fd back via reply_fd SCM_RIGHTS.
Worker now owns the only copy of the new socket fd.
SCM_RIGHTS: sock_fd (dup sent to each worker)
Manager closes its own copy of sock_fd.
Manager → Worker: status byte 0 (success) on reply_fd.

section.p: When a worker receives a broadcast socket fd via bcast_recv_handler, the C layer:
Creates a ngx_js_socket_state_t entry for the received fd.
Registers it in ngx_js_socket_reg[handle] and local_socket_reg.
Looks up nginx.onSocket in the JS global object.
If nginx.onSocket is a function, calls nginx.onSocket(sock) with a freshly-wrapped NginxSocket JS object.
This lets receiving workers act on the new socket immediately:

stanza.v: // Registered once in js_source (shared by all workers)
// sock is a fully usable NginxSocket in this worker
// e.g. start an accept loop, track it, close it, etc.

section.p: : nginx.onSocket is called synchronously within bcast_recv_handler. If it throws, the exception is logged and execution continues. The NginxSocket argument is a fresh JS object wrapping the same registry handle used by the sender.
Side │ Behaviour

Sender (Worker 0) │ broadcast() blocks (in C) until the manager has finished distributing the fd to all workers and sent its ack byte. The sendmsg to each worker via bcast_fds[wi][0] is non-blocking from the manager’s point of view, but the manager iterates all workers before replying.

Receiver (Worker N) │ The bcast_recv_handler fires when bcast_fds[wi][1] becomes readable — i.e. on the next epoll iteration after the manager’s sendmsg. This is asynchronous from the sender’s perspective. broadcast() returning in Worker 0 does NOT guarantee Worker N has already called nginx.onSocket.
If you need all workers to have acted on the socket before proceeding, combine broadcast() with suspendAllWorkers() / resumeAllWorkers():

stanza.v: // Suspend all workers so the bcast channel drains before
// any new connection is accepted on the new port
// Manager has sent fd to all workers; their event loops
// will drain the bcast fd before the first accept event
// fires, because accept events are suspended.

title.p: The bcast channel is activated lazily

section.p: The per-worker bcast fd (bcast_fds[wi][1]) is stored in w→bcast_fd at init_process. The epoll read event for it is not registered immediately — it is registered the first time a JS content handler runs via ngx_js_bcast_ensure_active(w). This means:

A broadcast sent before any request has been handled on Worker N will be buffered in the AF_UNIX socket kernel buffer. It will be delivered as soon as Worker N handles its first request (and activates the event).
The kernel buffer is large enough for hundreds of queued messages; in practice this is never a concern.
Condition │ Result
Called from config phase (master) │ Throws InternalError: sock.broadcast: only valid in worker processes
Socket already closed │ Throws InternalError: sock.broadcast: socket already closed or invalid
Manager not running │ Throws InternalError: sock.broadcast: manager failed to distribute socket to workers
Registry slot collision on receiver │ Logs WARN: bcast: handle N already occupied and discards the received fd

Adds a new virtual server to the HTTP subsystem.

stanza.v: nginx.http.addServer(name: string, opts?: { template?: string }): NginxServer

section.p: name — primary server name. opts.template — optional name of an existing server to copy configuration from (inherits proxy_pass, SSL, etc.). Defaults to an empty configuration.
The new server starts with an empty location tree. See Guide 5 [js-reconfig-guide-servers.adoc] for full details.

addServer() registers the server internally but does not update the server-name routing hash until rebuildVhostDispatch() is called. Incoming requests continue to use the old dispatch table until the rebuild.

section.p: Removes a virtual server from the HTTP subsystem.
Splices the named server from all internal virtual-host entries. Like addServer, the routing hash is not updated until rebuildVhostDispatch().

In-flight requests that are already executing inside the removed server’s handlers continue to completion. New connections will not be dispatched to the removed server after the next rebuildVhostDispatch().
Rebuilds the server-name routing hash from the current servers[] list.

Must be called after any addServer() or removeServer() to make the changes reachable by incoming requests. Safe to call at any time — the hash rebuild is an O(N) operation and completes in microseconds for typical deployments.
Simulates the full nginx dispatch logic and returns the server and location that would handle a given request.

nginx’s listening infrastructure is built incrementally. socket() bind() + listen() (Phase A) must happen before any process forks so all workers inherit the socket. Wiring the socket into the HTTP connection pipeline (Phase B) requires HTTP core data structures that exist only after http {} has been parsed. Activating the listener (Phase C) pushes it to cycle→listening, which is read by the event loop at worker start. Adding virtual hosts (Phase D) builds the per-listener name hash.
Separating these phases gives precise control over when each piece of infrastructure becomes active.

Server-name routing uses a static hash table. Adding or removing a server requires rebuilding the entire hash. addServer() / removeServer() defer the hash rebuild so multiple servers can be modified in a single batch before a single rebuildVhostDispatch() call makes all changes visible atomically.
The variable map is populated at config parse time by all modules that register variables. It cannot be extended at runtime because the variable index is embedded in compiled location configurations.

After workers fork, the master’s network namespace is the only one that can bind() privileged ports. Phase F uses the manager thread (which runs in the master) as a proxy: the worker sends the address, the manager creates the socket, and returns the fd via SCM_RIGHTS. broadcast() then distributes it to sibling workers using the same mechanism.

title.p: broadcast() is synchronous, nginx.onSocket is asynchronous

section.p: sock.broadcast() blocks the calling worker’s C thread until the manager has sent the fd to all peer workers via bcast_fds[wi][0] and replied with a success byte. The manager’s sendmsg into each worker’s bcast pipe is non-blocking (fire-and-forget from the manager’s perspective). Receiving workers process the incoming fd the next time their event loop drains bcast_fds[wi][1], which happens on the next epoll iteration after broadcast() returns — not before.
If strict ordering is required (all workers must have the socket before any of them can accept on it), use withSuspendedAcceptance() to hold all workers' accept loops while the broadcast completes.

title.p: The bcast channel is a pre-fork socketpair

section.p: ngx_js_sw_manager_start() creates bcast_fds[wi][0..1] socketpairs for each worker before fork(). Workers inherit the read end ([wi][1]) on fork; the master (manager thread) keeps the write end ([wi][0]). This is a unidirectional, per-worker delivery channel for socket fds, suspend/resume control bytes, and other future broadcast message types. Because it uses AF_UNIX SOCK_STREAM the kernel buffers messages until the worker drains them, so messages are never lost even if the worker is busy.
